analysis.one_liner: Bars stock exchanges from trading a company's shares unless it certifies compliance with campaign-finance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill received no committee action and no vote after being referred to the House Financial Services Committee in January 2010.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Alan Grayson's bill would have changed securities law so that no national stock exchange could trade a corporation's shares unless the company certified in its registration and periodic reports that it was complying with the federal campaign-finance rules governing corporate contributions and expenditures as they stood for the 2008 elections. In effect, keeping access to public stock markets would have been conditioned on following the election-spending rules of the pre-2010 era. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and shareholders, who would get a built-in check that companies tapping public markets are not financing elections outside federal campaign-finance rules. The certification would be part of the public record filed with securities regulators.

how_it_helps.text: Every corporation registering a security on a national exchange would have to certify compliance with the Federal Election Campaign Act rules on corporate contributions and expenditures as they applied to the 2008 elections [S3].
The certification requirement would also appear in the periodic reports public companies already must file, keeping the statement current quarter to quarter [S2].
Exchanges could not effect trades in a corporation's securities without that certification, making market access itself the enforcement lever [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations, which would bear the cost of certifying and documenting compliance each quarter, and could lose exchange trading access if they did not or could not certify. Stock exchanges would shoulder the administrative burden of policing the new listing condition.

drawbacks.text: The bill pins the requirement to campaign-finance rules 'as such section applied with respect to elections held in 2008,' a fixed snapshot that would not automatically track changes in election law, creating ambiguity about what companies must certify [S3].

Conditioning exchange trading on a campaign-finance certification risks disrupting markets: any compliance dispute could effectively freeze trading in a company's stock, a cost that would fall partly on ordinary retirement and brokerage accounts.
A certification of compliance adds little unless backed by investigation; the bill creates a reporting duty but no new enforcement agency or penalty scheme beyond the exchange-listing bar [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea gives voters and shareholders a standing, checkable statement that companies using public markets follow campaign-finance law, and it uses an existing disclosure system rather than building a new one. The costs are real but modest in design terms: quarterly certifications and exchange administration. Its main weakness is that it fixes the rules to a single election year and offers no clear path for adjudicating disputed certifications, leaving the market bar blunt. Honest supporters would concede it is a disclosure lever, not a cure for campaign-spending law itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson introduced the bill in the House on January 13, 2010 [S1].
The bill's only action beyond introduction was referral to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day; no further action is recorded [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill died at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011 without a committee or floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations and stock exchanges are better off: no quarterly campaign-finance certification was added to their filings, and exchange listings carry no such condition.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the committee on which he served; no colleagues joined as cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat sponsored it, no member of either party cosponsored it, and the Democratic-run committee it was sent to never acted, so the bill never developed bipartisan or cross-party support in the record.

industries.note: They would have had to certify quarterly compliance with campaign-finance rules to keep their shares tradable on national exchanges, a compliance cost and a transparency requirement their filings do not currently carry. Companies spending on elections outside those rules could have been cut off from stock markets.

Exchanges would have gained a new gatekeeping duty — refusing trades in uncertified securities — bringing administrative burden and risk of lost volume, but also new regulatory obligations. Their interest lay in avoiding the requirement.
